corrective-exercise-posture-pain-evidenc.title: Does Corrective Exercise Fix Your Posture, and Does It Fix the Pain?
corrective-exercise-posture-pain-evidenc.summary: A 2026 review of 28 trials found corrective exercise clearly improves posture, but pain did not reliably improve. Here is what that means for you.
corrective-exercise-posture-pain-evidenc.text:
## The posture of our times

Look around any train carriage, office or café today. Heads lean towards screens. Shoulders curl forward. Upper backs round like question marks. We sit more than any generation before us, and we spend hours looking down at laptops and phones. Many of us end the day with a stiff neck, tight shoulders or a dull ache between the shoulder blades.

This common pattern has a name: upper crossed syndrome, or UCS. Some muscles in the neck, chest and upper back become tight and overworked, while others become weak and underused. Over time, this pulls the body into a forward head, rounded shoulders and a curved upper back, often with pain and stiffness along the way (Chang et al., 2023). The tight muscles typically include the upper trapezius, levator scapulae and chest muscles, while the weak ones include the deep neck flexors, middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids and serratus anterior. Interestingly, there are still no clear diagnostic criteria for UCS, and the main risk factor is simply holding the same posture for long periods (Chang et al., 2023).

The popular answer is corrective exercise: stretch what is tight, strengthen what is weak, and "fix" the posture. The promise sounds simple. Straighten the body, and the pain will go. A large 2026 study (Khorramroo et al., 2026) put that promise to the test, and the answer was not as simple as many hoped.

## A very old idea

The belief that the right movements can "correct" the body is not new. The ancient Greeks practised calisthenics, a word linked to strength and beauty, to train both body and mind. In the late 1700s, Swedish gymnastics teacher Pehr Henrik Ling built a system of equipment-free exercises to improve movement and prevent disease (Hoffman & Gabel, 2015). In the 20th century, Joseph Pilates called his method "corrective exercise" and believed it could fix bad habits in the body. Today's corrective exercise programmes grew out of this long tradition of mind–body training (Hoffman & Gabel, 2015).

## How the researchers tested it

Instead of running one new experiment, Khorramroo and colleagues (2026) gathered the results of many earlier ones. This is called a systematic review and meta-analysis, and it is one of the strongest types of evidence in health research.

They searched four large research databases and found 28 randomised controlled trials with 901 people who had upper crossed syndrome. In each trial, one group did corrective exercise and another group did not, or did something different. The exercise programmes varied a lot: some followed the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM) model, some focused on strengthening, and some took place in water rather than on land (Khorramroo et al., 2026).

The researchers looked at posture angles, pain, muscle activity, balance and everyday function. They also checked how well each trial was done and rated how confident we can be in the overall results (Khorramroo et al., 2026).

## What they found: posture yes, pain not so much

The good news: posture improved a lot. People who did corrective exercise ended up with a less forward head, less rounded shoulders and a straighter upper back. These were large changes, and they showed up in both teenagers and adults, and with both NASM-style and strengthening programmes (Khorramroo et al., 2026).

The surprise: pain did not reliably improve. When all the trials were combined, the corrective exercise groups did not have significantly less pain than the comparison groups. The small difference that did appear was not big enough to matter in daily life. The researchers rated this evidence as low certainty, because many trials had weaknesses and their results did not agree with each other (Khorramroo et al., 2026).

Other benefits were mixed. Standing balance improved a little, but balance during movement, muscle activity and arm function showed no reliable gains (Khorramroo et al., 2026).

In short, corrective exercise seems to be very good at changing how the body looks, but much less certain at changing how it feels.

These results come with some important nuances. "Corrective exercise" is not one standard programme: the trials used different exercises, durations and settings, and compared them with very different control groups, which blurs the combined result (Khorramroo et al., 2026). "No significant effect" does not mean nobody improved; it means the benefit was not reliable across studies. Most trials were also short, so we do not know how pain changes over months or years. Even so, the message is clear. Corrective exercises may improve a person's posture and appearance, but they may not significantly reduce pain, whether acute or chronic (Khorramroo et al., 2026). Pain is complex and biopsychosocial: it can come from stress, anxiety and a sedentary lifestyle, not just from how we hold our bodies. Posture may have had little to do with the pain in the first place. There is no perfect posture or perfect alignment, and chasing one is like chasing fairies. This fits a wider pattern in exercise research, where no single type of exercise, including Pilates or core stability, clearly beats the others for long-term low back pain (Hayden et al., 2021). Instead, resistance exercise performed with good form, combined with motivation, encouragement and reassurance, may bring greater rewards in rehabilitation and pain reduction. People need to hear that they are not falling apart, and that uneven or one-sided movement patterns are normal.

## References

- Chang, M. C., Choo, Y. J., Hong, K., Boudier-Revéret, M., & Yang, S. (2023). Treatment of upper crossed syndrome: A narrative systematic review. Healthcare, 11(16), 2328. https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare11162328
- Hayden, J. A., Ellis, J., Ogilvie, R., Malmivaara, A., & van Tulder, M. W. (2021). Exercise therapy for chronic low back pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Issue 9, CD009790. https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD009790.pub2
- Hoffman, J., & Gabel, C. P. (2015). The origins of Western mind–body exercise methods. Physical Therapy Reviews, 20(5–6), 315–324. https://doi.org/10.1080/10833196.2015.1125587
- Khorramroo, F., Rostami, M., & Jalili Bafrouei, M. (2026). Corrective exercises strongly improve posture but fail to produce consistent clinical or functional benefits in patients with upper crossed syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, 18, Article 302. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-026-01707-8

hypertrophy-research-lengthened-training.title: Training the Stretch: What Early Muscle Research Reveals About Recovery and Longevity
hypertrophy-research-lengthened-training.summary: Hypertrophy research began with recovery, not aesthetics. Here is how it explains why training muscles at long lengths protects function.
hypertrophy-research-lengthened-training.html:
Hypertrophy research is often assumed to belong to the gym floor, a subject for those chasing size alone. In fact, a substantial part of the early work was concerned with something quite different: recovery.

In the 1970s and 1980s, researchers attached small weights to the wings of chickens and quails so that the muscles were held in a stretched position for weeks at a time. There was no training and no active contraction, only sustained passive stretch. Even so, the muscles became thicker and longer. They did this by adding new sarcomeres, the basic contractile units of muscle, in a row along the length of the fibre. In effect, the muscle rebuilt itself so that it could cope with the stretched position rather than remaining overstretched.

This process has a name: sarcomerogenesis, the creation and serial deposition of new sarcomeres. When a muscle is stretched beyond its physiological limit, it responds by adding sarcomeres in series. The added sarcomeres reduce the stretch on each individual unit and gradually restore the muscle to its optimal working length, a process modelled over a period of about two weeks in a rabbit limb-lengthening study (Zöllner et al., 2012).

Later animal studies have built on this foundation. In adult quails, a weight equal to 10% of body mass was worn on one wing in 24-hour periods, separated by rest days. The stretched muscle increased in mass by about 53% and in length by about 26%, through enlargement of its existing fibres rather than the formation of new ones (Antonio & Gonyea, 1993). In adult rabbits, three weeks of incrementally applied static stretch lengthened the latissimus dorsi muscle and increased the number of sarcomeres in series by 25% (Cox et al., 2000).

This lengthening, known as longitudinal growth, matters because it allows a muscle to work properly across a wider range of motion. A muscle that adds sarcomeres in series is less likely to be left overstretched and weak at the end of its range.

The motivation behind these experiments was practical. Researchers wanted to understand how muscle might be protected in people who were injured, bedridden or otherwise unable to train. That was the original context of the work, and it is why much of what is taught in bodybuilding today has its roots in rehabilitation.

It also brings us back to training. When a muscle is loaded in its most lengthened position, we draw on the same adaptive effect that those early studies observed. Over time, the muscle adapts to longer lengths, remains stronger through a greater range and is better able to hold on to its function after injury or as we grow older. Growth in size is only one part of the benefit.

At REVIVE, this is why we pay close attention to range of motion and to loading muscles through their full length, whether the goal is rebuilding after injury, staying strong with age or training for performance.

References: Antonio, J., & Gonyea, W. J. (1993). Role of muscle fiber hypertrophy and hyperplasia in intermittently stretched avian muscle. Journal of Applied Physiology, 74(4), 1893-1898.

Cox, V. M., Williams, P. E., Wright, H., James, R. S., Gillott, K. L., Young, I. S., & Goldspink, D. F. (2000). Growth induced by incremental static stretch in adult rabbit latissimus dorsi muscle. Experimental Physiology, 85(2), 193-202. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-445X.2000.01950.x

Zöllner, A. M., Abilez, O. J., Böl, M., & Kuhl, E. (2012). Stretching skeletal muscle: Chronic muscle lengthening through sarcomerogenesis. PLOS ONE, 7(10), e45661. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0045661

upper-crossed-syndrome-neck-shoulder-pai.title: Upper Crossed Syndrome: Why Your Neck and Shoulders Ache, and What to Do About It
upper-crossed-syndrome-neck-shoulder-pai.summary: Stiff neck and tight shoulders after a long day at your desk? Learn what upper crossed syndrome is, what causes it and how exercise and physiotherapy can help.
upper-crossed-syndrome-neck-shoulder-pai.text:
If you spend long hours at a desk and finish the day with a stiff neck, tight shoulders or a nagging headache, you may be dealing with Upper Crossed Syndrome (UCS). It’s one of the most common postural problems, and the good news is that it responds well to treatment (Chang et al., 2023).

It’s also worth knowing that plenty of people have the posture associated with UCS without any pain or symptoms at all, and that’s completely normal. If you’re active, pain-free, and it isn’t affecting your daily life, there’s usually no need for any major intervention. It becomes worth addressing when it starts to impact your quality of life, for example through restricted movement, headaches, ongoing stiffness, or pain that disturbs your sleep.

## What is it?

In UCS, certain muscles become tight and overactive while others become weak, which can affect posture and how the joints move (Chang et al., 2023).

The name comes from the “X” shape these muscles form when you look at the body from the side. Tight muscles at the back of the neck and shoulders cross with tight muscles at the front of the chest and neck, and weak muscles at the front of the neck cross with weak muscles in the upper back:

- **Tight at the back:** upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals
- **Tight at the front:** pecs major and minor, sternocleidomastoid, scalenes
- **Weak at the front:** deep neck flexors
- **Weak at the back:** middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior

## The signs to look out for

Neck pain is the most common complaint, but UCS can also cause headaches, upper back pain, chest pain, tingling in the upper arms, and reduced movement in the neck or shoulders.

You might also notice it in the mirror: a forward head posture, rounded or raised shoulders, an increased curve in the upper back, or shoulder blades that stick out (Chang et al., 2023).

## What causes it?

The main risk factor is holding a poor posture for long periods, often linked to work. Long hours at a desk, repetitive tasks, and prolonged sitting or standing in awkward positions can all make it worse (Chang et al., 2023).

## What you can do yourself

- Check your posture regularly throughout the day and correct it.
- Stretch the tight muscles, especially the upper traps, levator scapulae and chest.
- Strengthen the weak ones, such as the deep neck flexors (chin-tuck style exercises), mid and lower traps, rhomboids and serratus anterior.
- Fix your workspace so you can sit in a neutral position, with a supportive chair.
- Use a foam roller to ease muscle tightness.

## Does it work?

A 2023 systematic review of 11 studies found that exercise-based programmes aimed at correcting posture and muscle imbalance reduced pain and improved neck disability and posture in people with UCS (Chang et al., 2023). Combined approaches tended to do best: in one trial, a multimodal programme of posture training, ergonomic advice, MET and stabilisation exercises outperformed MET alone, and another found supervised exercise more beneficial than unsupervised exercise.

It’s worth noting the studies were mostly small and short, so more research is still needed.

## The takeaway

UCS is caused by muscle imbalances from poor posture, but it’s very manageable. Small daily changes, a consistent stretching and strengthening routine, and support from a physiotherapist when needed can make a real difference to how your neck and shoulders feel.

## How we can help

At Revive Wellness, we use a combination of soft tissue mobilisation and other hands-on techniques to reduce tension and restore movement, and we design a specific exercise programme for you, including stretching, strengthening and stabilisation work for the neck and shoulder blades. Alongside this, we'll teach you how to manage your posture long-term. Sessions with us are one-to-one in a calm, private setting in Central.

_Neck and shoulders aching after work? Book an appointment and we will build a plan that suits you._

_Reference: Chang, M. C., Choo, Y. J., Hong, K., Boudier-Revéret, M., & Yang, S. (2023). Treatment of upper crossed syndrome: A narrative systematic review. Healthcare, 11(16), 2328. https://doi.org/10.3390/healthcare11162328_

knee-osteoarthritis-what-helps.title: Knee Osteoarthritis: Why Rest Isn't the Answer and What Actually Helps
knee-osteoarthritis-what-helps.summary: Living with knee arthritis? A review of 54 studies shows the right exercise eases knee osteoarthritis pain and makes walking and stairs easier.
knee-osteoarthritis-what-helps.text:
Knee pain is one of the most common reasons people book a physiotherapy appointment in Hong Kong. Knee osteoarthritis, often called knee arthritis or knee OA, is a leading cause of difficulty with walking and daily activities in older adults. It is also one of the most misunderstood conditions, and many people are told, or simply assume, that they should rest and avoid exercise. The best research we have shows that, in most cases, the opposite is true.

## What is knee osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It mainly affects the cartilage that covers the ends of the bones and the bone just beneath it, but it is a condition of the whole joint, including the joint lining, ligaments and the muscles around the knee. It is often called "wear and tear", but that is misleading: the knee is a living, adaptable joint, and it responds to the loads we place on it.

There is currently no cure for OA. The encouraging part is that factors such as weak muscles and low fitness can be improved with exercise, and that makes a real difference to how the knee feels and works.

Common signs include:

- Pain when walking, using stairs or getting up from a chair
- Increasing difficulty with daily tasks such as housework
- Stiffness after sitting or first thing in the morning
- Swelling, clicking or a feeling that the knee is weak or "tight"

## Don't let the scan scare you

X-rays and MRI scans often show "arthritis" or "degeneration" in people who have no pain at all, and the amount of change on a scan does not always match how much pain you feel. A scan is one piece of information. Your symptoms, strength and what you can and cannot do matter just as much.

## Why rest makes it worse

Resting a stiff, painful knee feels sensible, but long periods of rest weaken the muscles that support the joint. A weaker leg means the knee takes more load, and that usually means more pain. Gentle, progressive exercise helps the knee cope better with everyday life.

## What does the research say about exercise for knee arthritis?

Does exercise really help knee arthritis? Researchers have looked at exactly that question. A large Cochrane review (Fransen et al., 2015), one of the most trusted types of medical research, combined the results of 54 studies of people with knee osteoarthritis. People who followed an exercise programme (on land, not in water) were compared with people who did no exercise. Here is what the researchers found:

- **Less knee pain.** Pain was clearly lower after treatment, by about 12 points on a 100-point pain scale.
- **Easier daily life.** Walking, climbing stairs and other everyday tasks became easier, by about 10 points on a 100-point scale of physical function.
- **A better quality of life.** There was a small improvement, of about 4 points.
- **Benefits that last, if you keep going.** Less pain and easier movement were still there 2 to 6 months later, but the pain relief started to fade after about 6 months. That is a good reason to keep exercising rather than stop.
- **Safe for most people.** No serious side effects were reported. Some people did notice more pain in their back, hip or knee.

## Which exercise is best for knee arthritis?

- **Stronger legs and regular activity.** Exercises that strengthen the legs, and fitness exercise such as walking or cycling, are recommended by most guidelines.
- **You don't need one perfect exercise.** The review found little difference in pain relief or movement between strengthening, fitness exercise and walking programmes. Programmes that focused only on things like stretching, balance or coordination worked less well than strengthening and fitness exercise.
- **Doing it regularly, with guidance, matters most.** Exercising one-to-one, in a class or at home all helped. People tended to do better with more sessions with a physiotherapist or trainer, although the researchers could not say this was certain.

## What this means for your knee pain

Current guidelines, including those from NICE in the UK, also place education and exercise at the centre of knee osteoarthritis care, with weight management where it is relevant. In practice, we focus on:

- **Understanding the condition.** Knowing that OA is manageable, and that a flare-up does not mean damage, takes away a lot of fear.
- **A regular, progressive programme.** We build leg strength and fitness gradually and check your technique, so the programme is safe and keeps progressing.
- **Managing load, not avoiding it.** We adjust the amount, intensity and type of activity so you can stay active without constant flare-ups.
- **Your weight and daily habits.** Even modest weight loss can reduce load on the knee. Footwear, stairs and long periods of sitting can also be addressed.
- **Hands-on treatment as a helper.** Manual therapy can ease pain and stiffness so you can exercise more comfortably, but it works best alongside exercise.

## Is there a cure for knee arthritis? What about stem cell injections?

Not yet. There is currently no treatment that has been proven to cure knee osteoarthritis or reverse the wear in the joint. That is why treatment focuses on easing pain and keeping you moving, and why exercise sits at the centre of it.

You may have heard about stem cell injections and other "biologic" treatments, such as platelet-rich plasma (PRP). Research into them is growing, and some studies report short-term pain relief. But the evidence is still limited, the studies are small and use very different methods, and there is no proof that these injections rebuild cartilage. They can also be expensive, and you may need repeat treatments. The American College of Rheumatology and the Arthritis Foundation, after reviewing the evidence, "strongly recommend against" stem cell and PRP injections for knee and hip osteoarthritis (Kolasinski et al., 2020). This may change as better research comes in, so it is worth asking your doctor what is currently supported.

## How do we measure progress? More than pain and quality of life

Pain scores and quality-of-life questionnaires matter, but they are not the whole picture. Two people with the same pain score can have very different strength and movement. Other useful ways to track how your knee is doing include:

- **Strength.** Weak thigh muscles are common with knee arthritis, and strength is one of the things exercise can improve.
- **Everyday function tests.** How quickly you can stand up from a chair several times, how fast you can walk, how comfortably you manage stairs, and how well you balance.
- **Knee movement and swelling.** How far the knee bends and straightens, and whether it swells after activity.
- **Your own goals.** Walking further, playing with the grandchildren, or getting back to hiking.
- **Body scans such as DEXA.** A DEXA scan is a low-dose X-ray that measures bone density and body composition, meaning how much muscle and fat you carry. It does not diagnose knee arthritis, but it can show whether your bones and muscle mass are healthy, which matters when planning strength training, especially as we get older. In a large US study of older adults (Misra et al., 2019), researchers used whole-body DEXA scans to measure muscle and fat mass and followed their knees over 5 years. Carrying excess body fat, especially with low muscle, was linked to a higher risk of developing knee arthritis, while low muscle mass on its own was not. Ask your doctor whether a scan is right for you.
- **X-rays and MRI.** These show the structure of the joint, but a review of the research (Bedson and Croft, 2008) concluded that knee X-ray results "should not be used in isolation when assessing individual patients with knee pain". How a knee looks on a scan does not always match how it feels or how well it works.

## When to consider other options

If your pain keeps you from sleeping, work or normal life despite a good period of rehabilitation, speak to your doctor. Medication, injections or an orthopaedic opinion can help in some cases, and joint replacement is an option when other treatments are no longer enough. Rehabilitation before surgery also tends to help recovery afterwards.

Seek medical advice promptly if your knee becomes hot, red and very swollen, if you cannot put weight on it, if you have a fever, or after a fall or injury.

## How we can help

At Revive Wellness, we assess your knee, explain what is going on, and build a supervised programme around your goals, whether that is walking pain-free, climbing the stairs at home, or returning to hiking and sport. Sessions are one-to-one in a calm, private setting in Central.

_Not sure where to start? Book an appointment and we will build a plan that suits you._

_References: Fransen M, McConnell S, Harmer AR, et al. Exercise for osteoarthritis of the knee. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2015._

_Misra D, Fielding RA, Felson DT, et al. Risk of knee osteoarthritis with obesity, sarcopenic obesity, and sarcopenia. Arthritis & Rheumatology, 2019;71(2):232-237._

_Bedson J, Croft PR. The discordance between clinical and radiographic knee osteoarthritis: a systematic search and summary of the literature. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2008;9:116._

_Kolasinski SL, Neogi T, Hochberg MC, et al. 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee. Arthritis Care & Research, 2020;72(2):149-162._

strength-training-after-50.title: Muscle Is Medicine: Why Building Muscle Is the Secret to Ageing Well
strength-training-after-50.summary: Muscle is far more than show. It is a health marker that shapes how well you age.
strength-training-after-50.html:
In the world of modern bodybuilding, people tend to picture big muscles with limited mobility - all show and no function.

Many question the purpose and importance of building muscle, aka hypertrophy. Especially in Asia, where the social standard of beauty favors a slim, slender look.

But as mankind lives longer and modern society faces population aging, longevity is directly linked to how much muscle you have and how well you can preserve it.

Muscles are not just dumb objects clinging to bones. Muscle is a health marker. It reflects how well your body metabolizes energy, how well it responds to insulin and regulates blood sugar, and even how it supports cognitive function.

Our movements depend on muscles lengthening, shortening, and contracting isometrically. Our muscles respond to force and stress from gravity. How we use our muscles determines the outcome. For example, prolonged sitting causes muscle atrophy, while resistance training drives muscle growth. In short: use it or lose it.

When we move under specific loads, our muscles experience different types of growth. One fascinating aspect of our physiology is what happens in the lengthened position under load. During a stretch under load, our body experiences longitudinal growth - in simple terms, the muscle fibers grow longer near the tendons, close to the joint attachments.

In our next post, we'll talk about how longitudinal growth protects our tendons and why most bodybuilding research is actually based on rehab.

return-to-sport-after-injury.title: Back in the Game: How to Return to Sport After Injury Safely
return-to-sport-after-injury.summary: Sports injury rehab, return-to-play testing and reinjury prevention, explained by a Hong Kong physiotherapist.
return-to-sport-after-injury.html:
When people hear of football, rugby and other sports, a fair few will associate sports with injury, or recall the time they could have turned professional if it wasn’t for a devastating injury. When you watch football, after a collision, a team of physios and other members of the medical staff rush onto the pitch with their duffel bags filled with medical equipment.

From a physio’s perspective, we are the bridge between the medical doctors and personal training, facilitating everything from and in-between. We are required to have a medical background, such as anatomy, the healing phases of different connective tissue, therapeutic modalities and treatments, as well as knowledge about physical activity: how to apply the medical knowledge to real-world scenarios with the equipment we are given.

I’ll give you a brief example:

Picture this: you are in the middle of a match when your knee twists awkwardly beneath you. Within minutes it swells up, and your gut tells you this is bad. You cannot carry on, so you hobble off the pitch.

You go to see a doctor, who prescribes painkillers and anti-inflammatories, and refers you to physiotherapy. This is where we come in. A physiotherapist’s job is not just to assess the injury; it starts with listening to your story and what happened, and asking questions to get a clearer picture first. We may then guide you through some basic movements, assess your balance, strength and pain levels, and carry out special tests to confirm, or rule out, the cause.

We also have to communicate our findings and our thought process clearly with you, to keep the dialogue open and stop you from guessing or becoming even more worried. From there, treatment could range from controlling the swelling first, to reducing pain levels, to relaxing muscles that are guarding as a protective mechanism. It is also about calming your nerves and reassuring you that things are going to be fine.

After that, physiotherapy should mainly be about tailoring an exercise programme around your needs: neuromuscular control, balance, proprioception, agility, muscle strength and psychological readiness, pushing you to a reasonable limit each session.

But the journey doesn’t end there. Even after you get back to the sport you love, physio visits revolve around screening, your feedback on how your injury is coping and how you feel, and how we can work on prevention and stability, so that we can minimise the chance of going through all of this again.

Now you have a brief picture of the physio’s perspective, and of the client across the table. Of course, there are a lot of nuances in between, but you can see how a physio shouldn’t just make you lie down on the table for the entire session. It should be interactive, with mutual feedback, and progressive.

If you want to get the best out of your sessions, understand what is going on every step of the way, and be given honest, straightforward feedback and reassurance, then this is the place for you.

References

Himani, Sah, N.K.P., Trivedi, A. and Kanhaiyya (2025) ‘Role of physiotherapy in sports injury prevention and recovery: a comprehensive review’, International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology, 3(10). Available at: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396717975_Role_of_Physiotherapy_in_Sports_Injury_Prevention (Accessed: 15 October 2026).

prenatal-training-by-trimester.title: Pre-natal training: what is safe each trimester
prenatal-training-by-trimester.summary: Stay strong and comfortable through pregnancy.
prenatal-training-by-trimester.html:
For most healthy pregnancies, staying active is encouraged. Exercise can support strength, mood, sleep and preparation for birth. Every pregnancy is different though, so always check with your doctor or midwife before you begin or continue a programme.

First trimester

Many women feel tired or nauseous in these early weeks, so energy can vary from day to day. Continue activities you are used to, keep intensity comfortable, and focus on regular walking and moderate strength work.

Second trimester

Energy often returns. This is a good time to build strength in the legs, hips, back and upper body, practise breathing and begin pelvic floor awareness. As your bump grows, exercises are adapted to keep you comfortable and stable.

Third trimester

Training shifts towards maintaining strength, supporting posture and preparing the body for birth. Lower impact, slower tempo and more rest between sets are common. Your trainer will modify any position that feels uncomfortable or makes you dizzy.

Stop and seek medical advice if you notice

  • Vaginal bleeding or leaking fluid
  • Dizziness or feeling faint
  • Chest pain or unusual shortness of breath
  • Calf pain or swelling
  • Regular, painful contractions

After the baby arrives

Returning to exercise after birth should be gradual and guided by your healthcare provider. Post-natal training can rebuild core and pelvic floor function, posture and overall strength at a pace that suits you.
